concepts.name: Model Parallelism
concepts.definition: A technique to distribute a single neural network model across multiple accelerators (e.g., GPUs or TPUs) to overcome memory limitations.
concepts.intuition: Imagine a large puzzle that’s too big for one person to assemble alone—model parallelism is like giving different people different puzzle pieces to work on simultaneously.
concepts.importance: Enables training of models too large to fit in a single accelerator’s memory, unlocking larger and more accurate neural networks.
concepts.example: Splitting a 128-layer Transformer model across 4 GPUs so each handles 32 layers.

concepts.name: Pipeline Parallelism
concepts.definition: A form of model parallelism where layers of a neural network are divided into stages, and each stage is processed on a different device in sequence.
concepts.intuition: Like an assembly line in a car factory—each worker (accelerator) does one step, and cars (micro-batches) move down the line while workers operate in parallel.
concepts.importance: Reduces idle time between layers by overlapping computation across micro-batches, improving hardware utilization.
concepts.example: Four GPUs process four micro-batches in sequence: GPU1 processes micro-batch 1, then GPU2 takes over as GPU1 moves to micro-batch 2.

concepts.name: Micro-Batch
concepts.definition: A small subset of a mini-batch used in pipeline parallelism to enable overlapping forward and backward passes across different device stages.
concepts.intuition: Think of a conveyor belt with small packages—instead of waiting for the whole box to finish moving before starting the next, you send smaller boxes continuously.
concepts.importance: Enables pipelining by breaking large batches into smaller units that can be processed in sequence without blocking.
concepts.example: A mini-batch of 128 samples is split into 4 micro-batches of 32 samples each for pipeline processing.

concepts.name: Mini-Batch
concepts.definition: A subset of training data used in one iteration of gradient descent to compute gradients and update model parameters.
concepts.intuition: Instead of feeding the entire dataset at once (too slow), you feed small groups—like tasting a soup with a spoon instead of drinking the whole pot.
concepts.importance: Balances memory usage and gradient quality; foundational for stochastic optimization in deep learning.
concepts.example: Training on 10,000 images using mini-batches of 32 images per step.

concepts.name: Gradient Accumulation
concepts.definition: The process of accumulating gradients from multiple micro-batches before applying a single parameter update.
concepts.intuition: Like saving up coins in a jar—you don’t spend each coin right away, but wait until you have enough to buy something big.
concepts.importance: Ensures that the effective batch size remains unchanged even when splitting into micro-batches, preserving training stability.
concepts.example: Accumulating gradients from 4 micro-batches to compute one update equivalent to a batch size of 128.

concepts.name: Synchronous Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
concepts.definition: A training method where gradients from all micro-batches in a mini-batch are computed and then averaged before updating model parameters simultaneously.
concepts.intuition: All runners in a relay race must finish their leg before the team’s total time is recorded—no one gets to update until everyone finishes.
concepts.importance: Ensures consistent and deterministic updates regardless of pipeline depth, critical for reproducibility and scalability.
concepts.example: After processing 8 micro-batches, gradients are averaged and used to update weights in a single step.

concepts.name: Layer Partitioning
concepts.definition: The process of dividing a neural network’s sequence of layers into disjoint groups (cells) assigned to different accelerators.
concepts.intuition: Splitting a long recipe into steps—each chef handles one set of instructions, passing the dish to the next.
concepts.importance: Enables model scaling beyond memory limits and forms the structural basis for pipeline parallelism.
concepts.example: A 10-layer CNN split into 3 cells: Cell1 = layers 1-4, Cell2 = layers 5-7, Cell3 = layers 8-10.

concepts.name: Cell
concepts.definition: A group of consecutive layers in a neural network assigned to a single accelerator as a unit for pipeline parallelism.
concepts.intuition: Each cell is like a ‘mini-model’—a self-contained module that receives input, processes it, and passes output to the next cell.
concepts.importance: Provides modular abstraction for pipeline execution and enables load balancing across devices.
concepts.example: In GPipe, a cell might contain 32 layers of an AmoebaNet model running on one TPU core.

concepts.name: Re-materialization
concepts.definition: The technique of recomputing intermediate activations during backpropagation instead of storing them to save memory.
concepts.intuition: Instead of keeping every sketch you made while drawing a portrait, you re-draw the previous steps when needed to save paper.
concepts.importance: Reduces memory footprint during training, enabling larger models without requiring more hardware memory.
concepts.example: During backpropagation, GPipe recomputes activations from earlier layers instead of storing them in memory.

concepts.name: Computation Cost Estimation
concepts.definition: A function that predicts the computational workload (e.g., FLOPs or time) of each layer or cell to optimize partitioning.
concepts.intuition: Like estimating how long each step of a recipe will take so you can assign tasks evenly among chefs.
concepts.importance: Enables balanced workload distribution across accelerators to prevent bottlenecks in pipeline execution.
concepts.example: GPipe estimates that layer 5 takes twice as long as layer 4, so it groups layers to balance total cost per cell.

concepts.name: Pipeline Efficiency
concepts.definition: The degree to which pipeline parallelism minimizes idle time and maximizes accelerator utilization during training.
concepts.intuition: A well-designed pipeline is like a busy kitchen where every chef is always cooking something—no one stands around waiting.
concepts.importance: Directly impacts training speed; poor efficiency leads to underutilized hardware and longer training times.
concepts.example: GPipe achieves near-linear speedup across 8 accelerators because pipeline stalls are minimized via micro-batching.

concepts.name: Hardware Memory Limitation
concepts.definition: The constraint imposed by the finite memory capacity of accelerators (GPUs/TPUs) that limits model size during training.
concepts.intuition: Your phone can’t run a full PC game because it doesn’t have enough RAM—same idea for large neural nets on GPUs.
concepts.importance: The primary driver for model parallelism; without solving this, models cannot scale beyond a few billion parameters.
concepts.example: A 6B-parameter Transformer model exceeds the memory of a single TPUv3, requiring partitioning across multiple devices.

concepts.name: Task-Independent Model Scaling
concepts.definition: The ability to scale neural network models across different architectures and tasks using a single, generic framework.
concepts.intuition: A universal adapter that works with any plug—whether it’s a phone, laptop, or toaster—you don’t need different tools for each.
concepts.importance: Reduces development overhead and enables rapid experimentation across diverse domains like vision, NLP, etc.
concepts.example: GPipe scales both AmoebaNet (vision) and 128-layer Transformer (translation) using the same pipeline library.

concepts.name: GPipe Library
concepts.definition: An open-source pipeline parallelism library that enables scalable training of arbitrary neural networks by partitioning layers and using micro-batch pipelining.
concepts.intuition: A plug-and-play pipeline engine—you just feed it your network layers, and it handles the complex parallel execution for you.
concepts.importance: Democratizes large model training by abstracting away complex parallelism logic, making it accessible to researchers.
concepts.example: Researchers use GPipe to train a 6B-parameter multilingual Transformer without rewriting their model code.

concepts.name: Near-Linear Speedup
concepts.definition: The phenomenon where adding more accelerators reduces training time proportionally, almost matching the ideal speedup (e.g., 8x faster with 8 accelerators).
concepts.intuition: If one worker takes 8 hours to paint a house, eight workers (with perfect coordination) take about 1 hour.
concepts.importance: Validates the efficiency of GPipe’s design—proving pipeline parallelism can scale without significant overhead.
concepts.example: Training a 557M-parameter AmoebaNet on 8 accelerators completes in nearly 1/8th the time of using one.
